title: Binary Search
summary: Return the index of target in a sorted array of distinct values, or -1, in O(log n).
statement:
`nums` is sorted in ascending order and its values are distinct. Return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not there.

Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.

Indices start at 0. Because the values are sorted, comparing `target` with the middle element tells you which half can still contain it, so each step halves the search range.
constraints: `nums` is sorted ascending and has distinct values
hints: Compare target with the middle element. What does the result tell you about the half you can ignore?
Keep a search range [lo, hi]. If nums[mid] < target the answer is right of mid; if it is greater, left of mid.
Use lo <= hi as the loop condition and mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 to avoid overflow. Return −1 when the range is empty.
explain: 9 is stored at index 4 of `[-1,0,3,5,9,12]` (indices start at 0), so the answer is 4. Binary search finds it by comparing with the middle and discarding half of the array each step.

title: Search Insert Position
summary: In a sorted array of distinct values, return the index of target, or the index where it would be inserted to keep the order.
statement:
`nums` is sorted in ascending order with distinct values. If `target` is in the array, return its index. Otherwise return the index where it would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted.

Run in O(log n) time.
constraints: `nums` is sorted ascending and has distinct values
hints: Both cases ask the same question: what is the first index whose value is ≥ target?
Binary-search for that "lower bound". The insert position can be nums.length, so search the range [0, n].
With lo = 0, hi = n: if nums[mid] < target set lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. When lo == hi, that is the answer.
explain: 5 is already in `[1,3,5,6]` at index 2, so the answer is 2. If it were missing, the answer would be the index where it would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted.

title: First Bad Version
summary: Versions 1..n are good up to some version, then every later one is bad. Using the provided isBadVersion(v), find the first bad version with as few calls as possible. (The tests also tell the judge which version is the first bad one.)
statement:
You have versions `1, 2, …, n` of a product. At some point a bad version was released, and every version after it is bad as well. Find the first bad version.

You are given an API `boolean isBadVersion(int version)`. Call it as few times as possible. (The judge also passes the first bad version as `bad` so that it can answer `isBadVersion`; your code should not read it.)
hints: The versions look like good, good, …, good, bad, bad, … . You are searching for the boundary.
Binary search: if mid is bad, the first bad version is at mid or before it; if mid is good, it is after mid.
Use lo = 1, hi = n and keep hi = mid when mid is bad. Compute mid as lo + (hi − lo) / 2, because lo + hi can overflow an int when n is near 2³¹.
explain: Versions 4 and 5 are bad and 1 to 3 are good. Checking version 3 shows good, so the first bad one is later; checking version 4 shows bad, and it is the first. The answer is 4.

title: Sqrt(x)
summary: Return the square root of a non-negative integer x, rounded down, without using a built-in power or sqrt function.
statement:
Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the square root of `x` rounded down to the nearest integer.

Do not use built-in power or square-root functions such as `Math.sqrt` or `Math.pow`.

Rounding down means returning the largest integer `r` with `r × r ≤ x`. Use a type wide enough for `r × r` (a `long` in Java), since the square can overflow a 32-bit int near the top of the range.
hints: You want the largest integer r with r × r ≤ x. That condition is true for small r and false for large r.
Binary-search r in [0, x] (or [0, 46340], since 46341² overflows an int).
Compute mid × mid as a long, or compare mid <= x / mid, so the square never overflows.
explain: 2 × 2 = 4, so the square root of 4 is exactly 2. For a value like 8 the true root is about 2.83, and rounding down would also give 2.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
summary: In a sorted array (duplicates allowed), return [first, last] index of target, or [-1, -1], in O(log n).
statement:
`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain duplicates. Return the first and the last index at which `target` appears, as `[first, last]`. If `target` does not appear, return `[-1, -1]`.

Run in O(log n) time, so a linear scan over the duplicates is not enough.
hints: Do two binary searches: one for the leftmost occurrence and one for the rightmost.
Leftmost: the first index with nums[i] ≥ target. Rightmost: the first index with nums[i] > target, minus one.
If the leftmost index is out of range or nums[left] != target, return [-1, -1].
explain: The value 8 appears at indices 3 and 4 of `[5,7,7,8,8,10]`, so its first position is 3 and its last is 4: `[3,4]`. A value that doesn't appear would give `[-1,-1]`.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
summary: Each row is sorted and each row starts after the previous row ends. Return whether target is in the matrix, in O(log(m·n)).
statement:
Every row of `matrix` is sorted in ascending order, and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the row before it. Return `true` if `target` is in the matrix and `false` otherwise.

Run in O(log(m · n)) time.
hints: Read the matrix row by row: it is one long sorted list.
Binary-search over positions 0 … m·n − 1 of that imaginary list.
Position p is the cell matrix[p / cols][p % cols].
explain: Read row by row, the matrix is one sorted list `1, 3, 5, 7, 10, …, 60`. 3 is in the first row, so the answer is `true`.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated some number of times. Return its minimum in O(log n).
statement:
A sorted array of distinct values was rotated: some prefix was moved to the end, so `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`. It may also have been rotated by a full cycle and be sorted again.

Return the minimum value, in O(log n) time.
hints: The array is two sorted runs. The minimum is the first element of the second run.
Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop (and the minimum) is to the right of mid.
Otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left, so set hi = mid. Stop when lo == hi.
explain: `[3,4,5,1,2]` is `[1,2,3,4,5]` rotated three places. The minimum is where the order breaks, right after 5, so the answer is 1.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot. Return the index of target or -1, in O(log n).
statement:
A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown index, for example `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`. Return the index of `target` in the rotated array, or `-1` if it is not there.

Run in O(log n) time.

Rotation keeps the values in order but starts the array part-way through, so it consists of two sorted runs. Searching for a value that isn't present returns `-1`.
hints: At any mid, at least one of the two halves [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is sorted normally.
Find out which half is sorted by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid].
If target lies within the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.
explain: 0 sits at index 4 of `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`, so the answer is 4. At every step one half of the range is sorted, which tells you whether the target can be inside it.

title: Find Peak Element
summary: Return the index of any element strictly greater than its neighbours (treat the outside as −∞; neighbours are never equal), in O(log n). Any peak is accepted.
statement:
A peak is an element strictly greater than both of its neighbours. Treat the positions just outside the array as `−∞`, so the first or last element can be a peak. Neighbouring values are never equal.

Return the index of any peak; there may be several. Run in O(log n) time.
hints: If you stand at mid and the value to the right is bigger, keep walking right: you must reach a peak before falling off the edge.
So compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1] and keep the half that goes uphill.
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] set lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. When lo == hi you are on a peak.
explain: In `[1,2,3,1]` the 3 at index 2 is larger than both neighbours (2 and 1), so index 2 is a peak and the answer is 2.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
summary: Return the median of two sorted arrays taken together, in O(log(m + n)).
statement:
`nums1` and `nums2` are each sorted in ascending order. Return the median of all their values combined. If the total count is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

The intended solution runs in O(log(m + n)) time; merging the arrays is O(m + n).
hints: The median splits the combined values into a left half and a right half of equal size. You only need to choose how many of the left half come from nums1.
Binary-search i (taken from nums1) in the shorter array; then j = half − i come from nums2. The split is right when nums1[i−1] ≤ nums2[j] and nums2[j−1] ≤ nums1[i].
Treat out-of-range neighbours as −∞ and +∞. Once the split is right, the median comes from max(left sides) and min(right sides).
explain: Merged, the arrays are `[1,2,3]`. With an odd count the median is the middle value, 2, returned as a double: 2.0.
